title: The End of the Product Life Cycle

stages.title: The Death of a Cash Cow

parts.visual:
Every product eventually dies. The curve is inevitable: Introduction, Growth, Maturity, and Decline.

The Executive Challenge:
1. The Cash Cow: During the 'Maturity' phase, the product stops growing but prints massive profits. Executives use this cash to fund the future.
2. The Decline: A new technology appears. Sales plummet.
3. The Sunset: The painful process of permanently discontinuing a legacy product that millions of angry users still rely on.
parts.audio: Every product has a life cycle: Introduction, Growth, Maturity, and Decline. Executives must aggressively harvest profits during the maturity phase to fund the creation of the next product.

questions.question: Your flagship software is 15 years old. Sales are no longer growing, but it generates $500 Million in pure profit every year with almost zero marketing. What is this product in business terminology?
options: A 'Cash Cow'. You should cut all R&D funding for it, harvest the massive profits, and use that cash to fund highly risky new startups within your company.
questions.correct_answer: A 'Cash Cow'. You should cut all R&D funding for it, harvest the massive profits, and use that cash to fund highly risky new startups within your company.
questions.explanation: Cash Cows are the financial engine of major corporations. You milk them until they die.

questions.question: Listen to the CEO's painful announcement. What phase is the product entering?
questions.tts_text: We are officially 'Sunsetting' the 3G network next year. We understand some legacy customers still use it, but maintaining the old infrastructure is preventing us from investing in 5G.
options: The Decline/Sunset phase. Forcing the painful 'End of Life' execution to free up capital.
questions.correct_answer: The Decline/Sunset phase. Forcing the painful 'End of Life' execution to free up capital.
questions.explanation: Sunsetting a product always creates furious customers, but carrying legacy 'technical debt' will eventually sink the company.

questions.question: In the 'Introduction' phase of a product lifecycle, what is usually true about profits?
options: Profits are deeply negative. The company is burning millions on R&D, marketing, and customer acquisition just to prove the product works.
questions.correct_answer: Profits are deeply negative. The company is burning millions on R&D, marketing, and customer acquisition just to prove the product works.
questions.explanation: This is why startups need venture capital to survive the Introduction phase.

questions.question: What is the 'Innovator's Dilemma' regarding product life cycles?
options: They don't know what color to paint it.
The hesitation to launch a new, disruptive product because it will instantly kill the 'Maturity' phase of your current, highly profitable Cash Cow.
questions.correct_answer: The hesitation to launch a new, disruptive product because it will instantly kill the 'Maturity' phase of your current, highly profitable Cash Cow.
questions.explanation: This brings us full circle to Cannibalization. If you don't kill your own Cash Cow, a startup will do it for you.

pairs.match: A business or product that generates a steady return of profits far exceeding the amount of cash required to maintain it
The intentional phasing out or termination of a product or service
The implied cost of maintaining legacy infrastructure instead of upgrading to a better approach
The progression of a product through Introduction, Growth, Maturity, and Decline
